system.name: Mentat sector growth vs political spending study
system.description: An exploratory R regression family in C:/Users/pgoff/Mentat/sector_growth_study. It relates industry growth, election timing and expected party control to giving, partisan share and lobbying, and adds the 2022 weekly seat-gain test (SEATS-W). Results are reported trend-first.

components.name: Sector growth vs giving, partisan share and lobbying regressions
components.computes: log giving ~ sector FE + growth(t-1, t) + phase + tossup + trend; RShare ~ growth + Shift (P - RMajNow); log lobbying with an AR term.
components.method: Wild sector-cluster bootstrap with Holm adjustment; two-way cluster SE as sensitivity; FD sensitivity. Results: no stable partisan shift (-0.04, p .76); the lobbying lead flips sign under year FE; growth adds no adjusted R2.
assumptions: Expected control is known at the time (retrospective for 2023/2025)
empirical_questions: Does sector growth predict political giving after year fixed effects?
Does expected change in party control shift industry partisan giving share?
components.heading: Sector growth vs giving, partisan share and lobbying regressions

components.name: SEATS-W weekly seat-gain test (2022 House)
components.computes: Weekly D share of giving vs expected D seats gained: -3.47 pp per seat (House), block-bootstrap p .0086-.0174; Senate null.
components.method: Fixed-X block bootstrap (3 and 5 weeks), Holm; HAC as secondary. One election.
empirical_questions: Do corporate donors shift partisan giving toward the expected winner as forecasts move within a cycle (strategic access-seeking)?
components.heading: SEATS-W weekly seat-gain test (2022 House)

evidence.title: On the Use of Two-Way Fixed Effects Regression Models for Causal Inference with Panel Data
evidence.claim: The 2FE estimator equals a matching estimator whose adjustment set has |A_it| = |M_it| x |N_it| and can contain same-status mismatches, so its simultaneous adjustment for unit and time confounders 'critically relies upon the linearity assumption'. Unweighted 2FE is not in general equivalent to the multi-period DiD estimator; the equivalence is the commonly cited justification from the basic two-group, two-period case.
evidence.system_side: The study's base L-LV models use sector baselines plus controls; the robustness family adds R-yearFE (sector + year FE), R-logFE, R-FD and FDY (first differences + year effects, EXPLORATORY, descriptive). The L3-LV slope is +0.352 (n=77) in the original specification and -0.477 under sector + year FE (log-FE -0.006; FDY -0.537); these are the Codex review reference values the pipeline checks its run against (sgs_review.R:33-35), and the sign flip is recorded in the sector-growth lane memory file (not the project brain), whose lesson reads 'Never call a trend a finding before the year-FE and incremental-fit checks'.
evidence.transfer: Transfers in part. The paper covers a binary treatment only (its conclusion says so); the growth regressors here are continuous, so the mismatch and negative-weight algebra does not carry over directly. The general point does: a 2FE slope is a model-based weighted contrast whose causal reading depends on linear additivity, and one-way FE, two-way FE and first-difference fits target differently weighted contrasts. Extension to continuous treatments rests on the TWFE literature the paper cites, not on this paper. The panel is small (77 rows on the L3 base fit). The paper supports the study's existing caution (year FE as a check, no causal language); it does not make the year-FE coefficient the 'true' effect.

evidence.title: On the Use of Two-Way Fixed Effects Regression Models for Causal Inference with Panel Data
evidence.claim: The multi-period DiD estimator, where units switch in and out of treatment, equals a weighted 2FE estimator with weights W_it; some control observations receive negative weights when (2X_it - 1)(2X_i't' - 1) = -1, so unweighted 2FE is not the DiD estimator. The wfe R package implements the weighted estimators.
evidence.system_side: DECEL is a within-sector binary indicator (1 when growth is below its prior-year value in the same sector), which switches on and off across years. The DECEL-<base> tests add g_decel and g x g_decel to the base specification, i.e. sector baselines (one-way unit FE) plus controls; no sector + year FE DECEL variant was found in the registry. The pipeline's 'temporal support' diagnostic reports each year's share of the absolute OLS weight on an estimate, not signed per-observation implicit weights.
evidence.transfer: DECEL has the paper's binary, reversible treatment shape, but it is fit with sector baselines only, not two-way FE, so Theorem 1's 2FE/DiD negative-weight result does not apply as written; the one-way unit-FE matching result is in Imai and Kim (2019), which this paper extends. It would apply directly only if a sector + year FE DECEL variant were added. DECEL is also built from the growth regressor itself, not an assigned treatment. Any signed implicit-weight diagnostic or wfe/PanelMatch comparison would be new analysis: UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062), EXPLORATORY under the original-model contract.

evidence.title: The Effect of Political Advertising after Citizens United: Adjusting for Unmeasured Confounding in Marginal Structural Models
evidence.claim: Unit fixed-effects regressions are biased when treatment and time-varying covariates feed back on each other (citing Imai & Kim 2019 and Sobel 2012). The paper's remedy moves the fixed effects into a propensity model and requires a binary treatment that switches within units, a correctly specified parametric propensity model, and N and T growing together. Simulations use n of 200-3000 with T of at least 4; in the empirical panel, campaign windows run 8-40 weeks.
evidence.system_side: OLS of sector-year spending DVs (contributions_real_m; LobbyView lobbying for the L*-LV tests) on a growth term with sector FE plus controls (pres_year, midterm_year, exp_dem_house, exp_dem_senate), with year-FE variants (variant year_fe) and first-differences-with-year-effects (FDY) checks; inference is a wild cluster restricted bootstrap by sector, DESCRIPTIVE when only 2 sectors. Reference values in the Codex review file sgs_review.R: L3-LV coefficient +0.352 (n=77) becomes -0.477 with year FE, and the FDY coefficient is -0.537 over 71 adjacent pairs (window and sample as set in that test's spec).
evidence.transfer: Only the diagnosis transfers, not the estimator. The study's regressor is continuous sector growth with few sector clusters and annual T, so IPTW-FE cannot run: no binary within-unit-switching treatment and no feasible propensity model. Read the paper as support for not interpreting the L-LV coefficients causally. A sign flip under added year FE is consistent with feedback or time-varying confounding, so neither sign is causal. Applies to any sector-year panel where lobbying or giving is the outcome of a growth regressor that may itself respond to past spending.

evidence.title: Empirical Models of Lobbying
evidence.claim: Huneeus and Kim (2019; LobbyView-Compustat): 766 of 7,646 US public firms lobbied in 2017; lobbying firms have almost four times the revenue of non-lobbying firms; conditional on lobbying, the elasticity of lobbying to sales is around one. Using committee-assignment shocks for identification, a 10% increase in lobbying produces a 3% increase in revenue.
evidence.system_side: Sector-year regressions of giving and lobbying on lagged sector growth with year-FE variants; the cited code handles year-FE variants (no within-sector variation in sector-only regressions). The reported results (lobbying lead flips sign under year FE; growth adds no adjusted R2) are not visible at the code_ref and are UNVERIFIED here.
evidence.transfer: The review's figures are firm-level cross-sectional size elasticities and a firm-level revenue effect. They do not predict a within-sector growth-to-spending effect once year shocks are absorbed, so a sector-year null does not conflict with them. They should not be cited as support for a deep-pockets hypothesis at sector-year grain.

evidence.title: The partisan ties of lobbying firms
evidence.claim: House-majority ties raise contract-firm revenue in 12 of 13 tests; Senate ties in only 3 of 13. In the 2011 House-flip kernel-weighted difference-in-differences, lobbyists at Republican-aligned firms gained just over $10,000 for the year, and ousted Democratic-aligned firms lost more than $40,000 in annual revenue (stated per lobbyist for one year in the key findings). Outcome: revenue per lobbyist; 1,603 contract firms, 2008 Q1-2016 Q3. The 2015 Senate flip shows no significant effect.
evidence.system_side: SEATS-W keeps House and Senate on separate seat scales (sgs_seats.R:24). The brain records one election, the 2022 House, 17 weeks, 538 Lite: -3.47 pp in the Democratic share of giving per +1 expected Democratic seat (block-bootstrap p 0.0086 at 3-week / 0.0174 at 5-week blocks; Holm 0.034 / 0.070), with the Senate showing nothing. The result is EXPLORATORY.
evidence.transfer: The House-yes, Senate-null pattern in SEATS-W matches the paper's House-over-Senate pattern, which supports chamber-specific estimates. The paper does not predict SEATS-W's sign: it measures contract-lobbying revenue after control actually changed, by firm partisanship; SEATS-W measures the partisan share of giving as within-cycle seat forecasts move. It cannot be cited as evidence for access-seeking in SEATS-W. Both are single-episode designs.

evidence.title: The partisan ties of lobbying firms
evidence.claim: Firm ties to the House majority are worth approximately $5,000 to $6,000 per lobbyist per quarter in the six levels models (firm random effects, year fixed effects, 2008-2016, N = 33,243 firm-quarters, 1,603 firms); first-differences models give $1,800 to $5,000. Senate effects appear only with the time-fixed measure in the levels models and not at all in first differences.
evidence.system_side: The SHIFT spec (brain) regresses RShare = R/(R+D) of candidate giving on Shift = P - RMajNow (expected minus current Republican control), by recipient chamber. The SHIFT preview (2021-25 window) shows no stable partisan shift: chamber-stacked -0.04, p 0.76; House +0.68 is SATURATED (2023 vs 2025 only); Senate -0.16. The cited sgs_panel.R lines build the SHIFT tables (which store the Democratic share D/(D+R) and expected/current Democratic control), not the regression itself.
evidence.transfer: The outcomes differ: the paper measures who earns lobbying fees, not where giving goes, and the separate Furnas et al. paper on lobbying/PAC overlap reports minimal overlap between lobbying and campaign-spending organizations. A null SHIFT preview is not contradicted by a lobbying-firm revenue premium. If SHIFT is ever extended to lobbying, key it to realized House control with chambers stratified.

evidence.title: The Effects of Firms' Lobbying on Resource Misallocation
evidence.claim: Lobbying raises firm revenue. Table 2 (printed p.26): IV log-sales elasticity 0.319 for all years (SE 0.0754, first-stage F 14.30) and 0.227 for post-2007 (first-stage F 13.10). OLS 0.0436 (all years) and 0.0500 (post-2007). Firm, year and state-year fixed effects. N = 15,332 (all) and 8,796 (post-2007). The paper names column 4 (IV post-2007, 0.227) as its preferred estimate. The reverse effect of size on lobbying is listed as an open question in the Conclusion (printed p.33).
evidence.system_side: The L-LV family regresses sector LobbyView lobbying in real 2025 USD millions (dv lobby_lv_real_m, the de-duplicated primary column) on lagged sector growth. The log forms (R-log) are separate robustness fits, so the base model is in levels, not logs. The R-yearFE variant swaps national controls for sector and year fixed effects. The recorded result that the lobbying lead flips sign under year FE was not found in the sector_growth_study markdown files checked here.
evidence.transfer: Design warning only. If lobbying feeds revenue, a growth-to-lobbying regression is simultaneous, so OLS with fixed effects cannot sign the lead. The paper's IV is 4.5 to 7.3 times its OLS (0.227/0.0500 = 4.5; 0.319/0.0436 = 7.3), not 4.5 to 7. The paper uses Compustat public firms with federal LDA filings 1999-2015 and no trade associations, while the sector panel includes associations, so the effect size does not transfer. The paper does not say how it handles self-filer and outside-firm double counting; the text mentions only that about 85 percent of lobbying is outsourced.

evidence.title: Mapping the Ideological Marketplace
evidence.claim: Table 2 (PDF p.21) and text PDF p.22: labor PACs ideological -231022 vs investor -252936; corporate and trade PACs unconstrained investor -1687949 vs ideological -1694458. Text says the investor model stays on par with the ideological model for these PACs, which is why they are excluded from scaling. Individuals are best fit by the ideological model.
evidence.system_side: sgs_seats.R header defines SEATS-W estimand A: weekly Democratic share of giving on the prior week's change in expected Democratic seats, pp per seat, residual block bootstrap. The stated result (-3.47 pp per seat, p .0086-.0174, 2022; Senate null) was not found in the .md, .json or .csv files under sector_growth_study. The header marks SEATS-W NOT BUILT until 09 exists.
evidence.transfer: Bonica's tests are cross-sectional over 2004-2012 with static covariates, not within-cycle forecast movement. The paper is consistent with strategic re-allocation for corporate and trade PACs and not for individuals. The 2022 result is one election and stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it. If the giving series mixes individual employee gifts with PAC money, the paper predicts dilution.

evidence.title: Corporate lobbying, political action committees, and market concentration
evidence.claim: Lobby coefficient on ShareAssets is 0.0743 (SE 0.0094) with full controls and 0.0907 with none; ShareMcap 0.0804 and ShareSales 0.0759 at full controls. Industry and year FE, no firm FE. Full-control sample N = 116,242 firm-years (1998-2016). ShareAssets mean 0.0727, median 0.0010. Coefficients are level shifts in a 0-1 share.
evidence.system_side: The sector growth study runs sector-by-year regressions of LobbyView real dollars on growth and sector controls. Verified: L3-LV base coefficient 0.352 and year-FE variant -0.477 (sgs_review.R line 33), and the year-effects guard at sgs_estimate.R line 386. The clause that growth added no adjusted R2 was not located and is not asserted here.
evidence.transfer: The paper estimates a between-firm cross-sectional association within NAICS industries, with lobbying on the right-hand side. The sector study asks a within-sector, over-time question with lobbying as the outcome. The paper has no within-firm or within-sector-over-time evidence, so it cannot support the growth-to-lobbying lead. Pooled across industries, so label UNSTRATIFIED. Imai and Kim caution is the analysts own point, not the paper's.

evidence.title: Corporate lobbying, political action committees, and market concentration
evidence.claim: WinPAC 0.0620 (SE 0.0267, significant at 5 percent) and LosePAC 0.0404 (SE 0.0356, not significant) in the Table 7 region. The authors conclude contributions to winning candidates drive the PAC effect. The text reports no equality test of WinPAC against LosePAC.
evidence.system_side: sgs_seats.R defines the SEATS-W estimand A (EXPLORATORY): weekly Democratic share change regressed on the prior-week change in expected Democratic seats, with residual block bootstrap within cycle. The rel's -3.47 pp estimate and its bootstrap p-values were not located in the sector growth study folder and are not asserted here.
evidence.transfer: Bickmore classifies money by realised election outcome after the fact and does not observe donors' responses to forecasts, so it cannot show donors anticipate winners. WinPAC versus LosePAC is a significant versus non-significant comparison with overlapping intervals, so treat it as a hypothesis. The paper's outcome is firm share, not weekly Democratic share.

evidence.title: Lobbying ROI: An Analysis under the American Jobs Creation Act of 2004 (also: Measuring Rates of Return for Lobbying Expenditures)
evidence.claim: Logit (Table 3, N not stated): ln assets .415 (p<.001), pre-tax income indicator .729 (p=.001), OCF/sales 1.918 (p<.001), cash/assets .225 (p=.640); no industry indicator significant. OLS (Table 5, N=434, adj R2 .48): ln assets .915 (p<.001), cash/assets 3.702 (p<.001), OCF/sales 1.679 (p=.023), pre-tax income indicator -.314 (p=.330), SIC 3800 2.196 (p=.085).
evidence.system_side: sgs_config.R defines the four LDA and LobbyView dependent variables (general giving, outside-firm income, self-filer expenses, undifferentiated LobbyView) and records that the undifferentiated LobbyView sum double counts self-filer fees, with a median 9-26 percent by sector. The regression design and the claimed results (no stable growth effect; lobbying lead flips sign under year FE) sit outside the cited lines and were not checked.
evidence.transfer: These are firm-level predictors of capturing a 2004-2006 benefit in a cross-sectional design with no causal identification. They are weak support for a firm-size covariate and say nothing about sector-year giving or growth. Cite as single-era and cross-sectional. Any pooled coefficient over the industry fault line needs strata or an UNSTRATIFIED label.

evidence.title: Cross-Industry Political Spending - Analysis Overview (memo)
evidence.claim: The memo says industries adapt giving to executive-branch pressure regardless of party. Examples: Bank of America PAC spending rose and its partisan split became more balanced after the debanking dispute and DOJ probe; JPMorgan streamlined PAC giving after internal memos. The causal link is hedged ('most likely', lines 22 and 28). No counterfactual or test is given.
evidence.system_side: sgs_estimate.R lines 172-179 label the expected-minus-current House and Senate control terms and the presidential-year term. Lines 1-10 and 299-359 describe a wild cluster restricted bootstrap by sector. The Holm adjustment is not found in sgs_estimate.R. The SHIFT result of -0.04 with p .76 was not found in the sector growth study text searched, so that number is not confirmed here.
evidence.transfer: The memo concerns executive-branch pressure, while SHIFT concerns congressional control, so the two do not test the same thing. The memo offers firm-level anecdote with no counterfactual and cannot be cited as a finding. At most it motivates a pre-registered event study around dated enforcement actions.

evidence.title: Various Versatile Variances: An Object-Oriented Implementation of Clustered Covariances in R
evidence.claim: Eq 20 gives the two-way meat as G(id)/(G(id)-1) M(id) + G(time)/(G(time)-1) M(time) - G(id x time)/(G(id x time)-1) M(id x time). For Petersen firm+year the slope SE 0.053561 matches multiwayvcov only in the printed run with multi0 = TRUE; the text says the default Ma (2014) correction differs from multiwayvcov.
evidence.system_side: sgs_review.R crv() applies (G/(G-1))*((n-1)/(n-p)) to cluster score sums; two-way = crv(sector) + crv(year) - crv(sector x year); df = min(G_sector, G_year) - 1; a non-positive variance is reported as a note only, not repaired. No multi0 option exists in the code.
evidence.transfer: Formula is for OLS on the sector-year design. Equivalence with sandwich::vcovCL on the study design is not run, so it stays UNVERIFIED (DE-062). The paper's multi0 advice applies when each sector-year cell holds one observation; whether the study's cells are singletons was not checked.

evidence.title: Various Versatile Variances: An Object-Oriented Implementation of Clustered Covariances in R
evidence.claim: Exp IV (Fig 4, rho = 0.25, G = 10 to 250): at G = 10 clustered SEs are underestimated in most cases, with HC3 the exception for binomial and Poisson; about 50 to 100 clusters suffice for CL-0. Separately, Sec 5.2 cautions that the Petersen year dimension has only 10 clusters.
evidence.system_side: sgs_review.R computes the two-way CR1 only when both dimensions have at least 3 clusters (SGS_TWOWAY_MIN_CLUSTERS = 3), with t on min(G_sector, G_year) - 1 df, labelled a sensitivity. DEFAULT_WINDOW is 2020-2025 (about 6 years; 2026 partial and excluded by default). Nine study sectors are listed in sgs_config.R.
evidence.transfer: The paper's simulations are balanced clusters of 5 with Gaussian-copula correlation, not two-way designs. The direction (SEs too small below G = 10) transfers qualitatively; the size of the bias for the study's sector x year design is not measured. The analyst's 9 x 4 design is not traced in code.

evidence.title: Various Versatile Variances: An Object-Oriented Implementation of Clustered Covariances in R
evidence.claim: Exp IV: for small G the coverage order is HC3 best, then HC2, HC1, HC0. The authors say their results are not consistent with HC3 being overly aggressive, though HC3 slightly over-corrects at G = 10 for binomial. The clustered bootstrap (R = 250) is somewhat better than HC0 and HC1 at small G. Pustejovsky and Tipton (2018) is cited as recommending HC2 with Satterthwaite t.
evidence.system_side: sgs_estimate.R: WCR bootstrap-t with Webb six-point weights, clusters = sectors, CR1 factor G/(G-1)(n-1)/(n-p) in the t statistic (sgs_cr1_factor). A grep of sgs_review.R and sgs_estimate.R finds no CR2 or CR3 error.
evidence.transfer: The paper's bootstrap is a clustered bootstrap with R = 250; its resampling type is not stated for the simulations, and wild or Webb bootstrap-t is not tested. So the paper cannot rank WCR against CR2 or CR3. The HC3 ranking is for linear and GLM fits with balanced clusters of 5, not two-way designs with about 9 sector clusters.

evidence.title: Various Versatile Variances: An Object-Oriented Implementation of Clustered Covariances in R
evidence.claim: Panel PL and PC coverage is poor with short panels (5 observations per cluster) and with exchangeable correlation, where coverage falls as panels lengthen. With decaying AR(1) correlation, coverage rises toward 0.95 as panels lengthen. The paper says some care is needed with panel estimators in short panels or with non-decaying autocorrelation.
evidence.system_side: sgs_seats.R: primary inference is a fixed-X residual moving-block bootstrap within cycle (3 and 5 weeks, Holm within family). Newey-West HAC with Bartlett lags 2, 4 and 8 is a secondary check and carries no p-value.
evidence.transfer: The paper's panel estimators apply to many short clusters. SEATS-W is one weekly series inside each cycle with no cluster dimension, so only the general point transfers: HAC is fragile when dependence does not decay. The paper gives no evidence on a single series.

evidence.title: Object-Oriented Computation of Sandwich Estimators
evidence.claim: Meat is the outer product of estimating functions with optional n/(n-k) adjustment (Eq. 10, p.6); sandwich errors lose power under correct specification and are useful only if estimates stay consistent; probit age p moves from .033 to .051 (n = 601, Sec 5.2).
evidence.system_side: OLS with sector baselines reports HC1 = (n/df) A X'uu'X A as a reference-only error (sgs_estimate.R lines 35-36); CR1 at sgs_estimate.R lines 44-45; primary inference is a wild cluster restricted bootstrap-t with a t_cr1 statistic (header lines 1-12, sgs_estimate.R line 264).
evidence.transfer: HC1 and CR1 formulas match Eq. 10 with cluster sums added. The paper's meat assumes independent rows, so within-sector dependence needs CR1, which the paper does not treat. Statsmodels cross-check is in code/tests/test_estimate.py lines 44-45, not tests/ at repo root.

evidence.title: Object-Oriented Computation of Sandwich Estimators
evidence.claim: HAC meat is a weighted sum of lagged estimating-function cross-products (Eq. 11, p.7) behind NeweyWest-type wrappers; no coverage study is reported, and Kiefer-Vogelsang fixed-b testing is named as an alternative (Sec 6, p.14).
evidence.system_side: SEATS-W computes Bartlett Newey-West HAC by hand at lags 2, 4 and 8 weeks within cycle with weights 1 - l/(L+1) and n/(n-p) (sgs_seats.R line 277 and lines 389-400); reported as secondary with no p-value. Primary inference is a residual moving-block bootstrap with fixed regressors, plus a recursive block bootstrap for dynamic models.
evidence.transfer: Lags, Bartlett weights and n/(n-p) factor match the paper's Eq. 11 setup. The paper gives no finite-sample guarantee, so the caveat that HAC is secondary applies. The 17-week figure appears in the code comment at sgs_seats.R lines 71-77 as an example of an interval, not as a stated cycle length. No second-path check against sandwich::NeweyWest was found in code/tests.

evidence.title: Econometric Computing with HC and HAC Covariance Matrix Estimators
evidence.claim: Eq. 6 HAC is a weighted sum of lagged products of estimating functions. Investment example RealGNP SE is 0.0168 (Newey-West lag 4, no prewhitening), 0.0236 (Newey-West automatic bandwidth with prewhitening) and 0.0208 (Parzen kernel, VAR(2) prewhitening, no finite-sample adjustment). Spread about 40 percent (0.0236 vs 0.0168). Coefficient 0.1691 is significant under all three; paper says the estimators give slightly different SEs but agree on the conclusion.
evidence.system_side: SEATS-W hand-codes a Bartlett Newey-West SE at fixed lags 2, 4 and 8 weeks, lag pairs matched within cycle by calendar week, n/(n-k) adjustment, no prewhitening and no automatic bandwidth, labelled secondary with no p-value. Primary inference is a fixed-X moving-block bootstrap with Holm.
evidence.transfer: Paper examples are time series; RealInt has 103 quarterly obs (1961(1)-1986(3)); Investment length is not stated in the text (fitted series starts 1964). The text does not call the series stationary and gives no coverage evidence at weekly-panel sizes. The ~40 percent spread supports showing several lag settings, not validating any one lag.

evidence.title: Econometric Computing with HC and HAC Covariance Matrix Estimators
evidence.claim: HC variants use the sandwich form (X'X)^-1 X' Omega X (X'X)^-1 with diagonal Omega weights built from residuals and the hat-matrix diagonal; HC0 to HC4 differ only in these weights.
evidence.system_side: sgs_estimate.R hand-codes an HC1 sandwich V = (n/df) A X'uu'X A, labelled reference only. DESCRIPTIVE tests report the estimate and the HC1 error only; inference is a wild cluster restricted bootstrap with Webb weights. The Holm step was not seen in this file.
evidence.transfer: Context only. Any HC3 column for DESCRIPTIVE fits is an UNVERIFIED suggestion until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).

evidence.title: Small Campaign Donors
evidence.claim: Weekly giving is dominated by calendar and event shocks. 30 of 31 abnormal weeks for large donors coincide with quarterly deadlines, against 27 of 43 for small donors. The week of Justice Ginsburg's death carried 13.0 percent of 2020 small-donor contributions versus 5.9 percent for large donors.
evidence.system_side: sgs_seats.R:511-515 builds a formula of the form y on a focal term plus a base term. For multi-cycle level models the base is cycle fixed effects plus cycle-specific linear week-of-cycle trends. Single-cycle models use one common week trend. Change and lag variants exist. No quarter-end or salient-event term appears in these lines. The outcome definition (D share of giving) was not traced.
evidence.transfer: Relevant only if the weekly series includes individual employee receipts and if deadline or event surges differ by party. Dobbs in 2022 is an example event. A quarter-end and event-week sensitivity is a candidate check, not a demonstrated bias. Unverified agent analysis (DE-062).

evidence.title: Why Is There So Little Money in U.S. Politics?
evidence.claim: In the gubernatorial panel (N = 326, state FE) the income elasticity of spending is 1.07 and 1.17 across Table 3 specifications, and per-capita state government spending has no independent effect (-0.09). Real campaign spending roughly doubled 1976-2000 but shows no trend relative to national income. 94 top executives at 12 large firms gave about 7500 dollars per cycle, or 51 dollars per 100000 of annual compensation (0.05 percent), against 0.04 percent of national income in 2000.
evidence.system_side: sgs_config.R lines 67-76 define the job tiers and NATIONAL_VARS (presidential and midterm year, party control, seat forecasts, GB538 margin). No income term appears there. The study's own result (no stable growth effect, no adjusted R2 gain) was not checked in this pass.
evidence.transfer: The paper's units are states and aggregate federal spending, not industry sectors. The consumption account predicts that employee and executive giving follows donor income rather than industry fortunes, consistent with the study's null. A real-dollar trend may partly reflect income growth. The executive figure is a share of compensation, which the paper says overstates the income share.

evidence.title: Difference-in-Differences with a Continuous Treatment
evidence.claim: The TWFE slope on a continuous dose is a weighted integral of ATT(d|d). In the levels form the weights integrate to zero and are negative for doses below the mean dose (Thm 3.4b). Under PT the causal-response form is a convex average of ACRT(d|d) plus a selection-bias term (Thm 3.4a). With no untreated units only differences relative to the lowest dose are identified (Remarks 3.1, 3.2). Application: TWFE 1.14 (s.e. 0.099), ATT_loc 0.80 (s.e. 0.05), ACRT_glob -0.08 (s.e. 0.19); dropping untreated units shrinks TWFE by 78 percent; recoding dose from 0-1 to 0-100 shrinks it to 0.0114.
evidence.system_side: sgs_registry.R:31 defines the growth regressors (growth_previous_year_pct, growth_same_year_pct, predicted_growth_pct). Robustness tests R-yearFE-* and R-logFE-* replace the national controls with sector plus year fixed effects (sgs_registry.R:664-671). Sector-only fits with year effects are labelled UNSTRATIFIED because no sector-only estimate exists (sgs_estimate.R:254-255, reason at 385-398). The primary specifications were not fully traced here, so sector-plus-year is confirmed only for the robustness variants. In the latest run (summaries_analysis-R-20260926T221444Z.txt) the L1-LV year-FE growth coefficient is -0.0014 (s.e. 0.123) with adjusted R2 0.8863 with the term and 0.8874 without it. The claim that the lobbying lead flips sign under year FE was not checked.
evidence.transfer: The paper's formal results cover two-period and staggered absorbing doses. Sector growth is non-absorbing and changes every year, so the decomposition does not carry over exactly; the de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille estimators the paper cites fit that case. The qualitative lesson transfers: a null or sign-changing pooled growth slope under FE can reflect implicit weighting across sector-years and heterogeneous sector responses, not only zero response. Window and denominator: sector-years in each test's gated sample.

evidence.title: Advancing the Empirical Research on Lobbying
evidence.claim: Kerr, Lincoln and Mishra as cited: a firm that lobbied last year lobbies this year with 92 percent probability (firm-level, federal). Within-group variation in lobbying is little, so fixed-effects designs need external shocks; omitted channels and endogenous selection into lobbying bias naive estimates.
evidence.system_side: Brain topic note: L3-LV coefficient +0.352 becomes -0.477 with sector and year fixed effects; growth adds no adjusted R2 (0.884717 vs 0.884690); first-difference with year effects -0.537 over 71 pairs.
evidence.transfer: The 92 percent is a firm-level federal figure, not a sector-year figure. The essay gives no sign for any sector coefficient, so the sign reversal is a fixed-effects fragility the essay anticipates, not validation of either sign. Figures must name window and denominator.

evidence.title: The Dynamics of Firm Lobbying
evidence.claim: Short panel (T=9, 1998-2006). Within-firm FE OLS gives 0.44 (column 7; column 8 gives 0.34), which the authors expect to be biased downward following Nickell 1981. Blundell-Bond GMM with lag-two instruments gives 0.84-0.88 (columns 2-6). Arellano-Bond is more sensitive across variants; its point estimate is 0.52 (SE 0.18) in Appendix Table 3 column 2, which the analyst omitted.
evidence.system_side: Brain sector-growth topic (line 269) transcribes the original contract equation (3) as log Lobby = alpha_i + rho times lagged log Lobby + growth terms + phase terms, with 5 sector clusters noted. The claim that implemented core L tests are levels with sector FE and no lagged outcome, and that only SEATS-W carries a lagged-outcome sensitivity, was not verified line by line in sgs_registry.R.
evidence.transfer: The Nickell-bias order (1+rho)/(T-1) is a textbook approximation, not a Kerr result; applying it to Mentat is new agent analysis and stays UNVERIFIED (DE-062). The claim that GMM is not feasible with 5 clusters has no source in Kerr or the brain and was not verified.

evidence.title: The Dynamics of Firm Lobbying
evidence.claim: Mean annual sales 5,407 ($m) for lobbying firms vs 1,423 for non-lobbying firms (Table 1; 327 lobbying firms of 3,260, 1998-2006). Policy response identified from 2001 dependence times a 2004-2006 binding-cap dummy with firm and year FE; high-skilled lobbying 0.043 (SE 0.014) per log LCA count (Table 5, 846 core obs). Falsification on unrelated issues is null (pp.15-16).
evidence.system_side: Growth adds no adjusted R2: 0.884717 with predicted growth vs 0.884690 without, on 77 rows (Codex review note in sgs_review.R line 237, also in brain). L3-LV growth coefficient flips from +0.352 to -0.477 with sector and year FE (brain). Both confirmed.
evidence.transfer: Kerr shows size predicts who lobbies, and that the 2004 response came from already-lobbying firms changing issues. Kerr does not show that yearly changes follow shared issue shocks, which the analyst text claims. A dated CU or bank policy design would be a new preregistered estimand, not a rescue of the growth tests.

evidence.title: Wild Bootstrap Inference for Wildly Different Cluster Sizes
evidence.claim: With unequal state-sized clusters (G = 50, Table 2) CRVE t(G-1) rejection at nominal .05 runs from 0.0567 to 0.1078 across the rho grid (0.10718 at rho_eps 0.9, rho_x 1); at G = 100 (Table 4) it reaches 0.08442; the restricted wild cluster bootstrap stays between 0.04905 and 0.05277 (Table 2). The conclusion recommends WCR over t(G-1) and says G* critical values often improve matters but do not always work as well.
evidence.system_side: Focal coefficients are tested with a wild cluster restricted bootstrap-t, null imposed, CR1 SE in the statistic, symmetric two-sided p, test-inverted 95 percent CI, B = 9,999 or full enumeration. Clusters are sectors for sector-year tests but champions (bioguide) for the H5 tests, so the analyst's sector-only system_side is overbroad.
evidence.transfer: The paper's size evidence is for Rademacher weights. The study uses Webb six-point weights, which this paper does not evaluate; it only cites Webb (2014) for G below about 12. Paper designs are linear models with G from 12 to 200. Whether the study's sector cluster sizes are near-balanced was not checked against study data in this pass; H5 bioguide clusters are the likely unequal-size case.

evidence.title: Wild Bootstrap Inference for Wildly Different Cluster Sizes
evidence.claim: The paper says Rademacher weights should not be used when G is below about 12 and points to Webb (2014) for that regime, but does not itself test Webb six-point weights. Its evidence starts at G = 12 (Appendix A.6 uses G = 12, 16, 20, 25, 32; Sections 6 and 7 use larger G). It says the exact G1 cutoffs for safe bootstrap inference are data dependent.
evidence.system_side: The study clusters by its nine sectors (config STUDY_SECTORS lists nine), uses Webb six-point weights with exact enumeration when 6^G is at most 9,999, requires at least 3 sector clusters for LobbyView bootstrap inference (DESCRIPTIVE below), and prints the 2/6^G p floor for DESCRIPTIVE tests. MIN_SECTORS is 2, so runs with 2 clusters are possible in code.
evidence.transfer: The paper gives no rejection rates at G of 3 to 9 and no evidence on six-point weights. Bootstrap p-values at 3 to 9 sectors are therefore unverified by this paper and need the study's own placebo or simulated-null check, or Webb (2014), before being read as correctly sized.

evidence.title: Wild Bootstrap Inference for Wildly Different Cluster Sizes
evidence.claim: With G1 = 1 (one treated cluster among 50 equal-sized clusters), the CRVE t(G-1) test rejects 77.75 percent of the time at .05, and the restricted wild bootstrap never rejects at any conventional level in these experiments. For equal-sized DiD the paper says the bootstrap can probably be used safely for 7 <= G1 <= G-7 and is likely misleading below 4 or above G-4.
evidence.system_side: Per-sector terms resting on one sector cluster and saturated SHIFT terms are labelled DESCRIPTIVE with bootstrap lines as reference only. The review adds each year's share of absolute OLS weight for each focal term.
evidence.transfer: The paper's G1 is a count of treated clusters for a binary DiD regressor. For continuous growth terms the analogue is how concentrated OLS weight is across sectors; the study reports this per year but not per sector. The 4-to-7 cutoffs are for the bootstrap in equal-sized DiD and do not transfer as numeric cutoffs to continuous terms.

evidence.title: Wild Bootstrap Inference for Wildly Different Cluster Sizes
evidence.claim: Conclusion: cluster-robust t inference should not be trusted even when the sample is large and the rule of 42 is satisfied, because overrejection with wildly unequal cluster sizes is serious; the paper's results are for one-way clustering.
evidence.system_side: The two-way sector-by-year CR1 SE with min(G_sector, G_year) - 1 df is computed only as a sensitivity when both dimensions have at least 3 clusters, and is explicitly not the study's inference.
evidence.transfer: The paper tests one-way clustering only, so the claim that the two-way CRVE inherits the t(G-1) warning a fortiori is the analyst's reasoning, not a paper result. The about 7 years figure was not checked against study data.

evidence.title: Partisan Impacts on the Economy: Evidence from Prediction Markets and Close Elections
evidence.claim: Table 2 daily-close campaign regressions give S&P coefficients 0.087 (daily), 0.128 (5-day) and 0.243 (20-day); oil -7.269 (5-day) and -12.570 (20-day). Text says the Table 2 equity effect is roughly a factor of ten larger than Table 1 (0.016 at 10-min differences, n=104). Authors attribute the gap to bias from reverse causation and common shocks. The OLS upper-bound statement (p.11, fn 14) concerns the reverse regression of the Bush probability on the S&P (2.3 and 3.3 pp per 10 percent rise), and holds if the shock correlation is non-negative, a sufficient condition.
evidence.system_side: SEATS-W regresses the week's Democratic share of giving on the prior week's change in 538 expected Democratic seats, pairing each week with the latest forecast available strictly before the week starts. 2022 House, 17 weeks, -3.47 pp per seat, EXPLORATORY. The code header presents it as a correlation and does not address common shocks.
evidence.transfer: The size of the bias does not transfer to PAC giving (lumpy, deadline-driven, different series), but the existence of a common-shock confound does: the as-of lag removes within-week ordering, not shared news moving forecasts and giving together. The negative slope cannot be read as donors moving toward or away from the expected winner. An upper-bound argument needs a stated correlation sign, which SEATS-W does not supply.

evidence.title: Partisan Impacts on the Economy: Evidence from Prediction Markets and Close Elections
evidence.claim: Identification uses two discrete election-night jumps in the Bush probability: the 2004 exit-poll leak (about 55 to 30 percent, then 95) and the 2000 Florida calls. Equity effects are 10- and 30-minute regressions (Table 1); a Wald estimator is stated explicitly only for yields (TIP and IEF, p.8-9). Footnote 9 splits the sample at 8pm and 10pm to test feedback. The paper does not recommend event-window designs; footnote 13 names instrumental variables as the ideal and leaves it open.
evidence.system_side: SEATS-W uses every pre-election week as an observation, with a residual block bootstrap conditional on the forecast path. No event-window design around large forecast moves exists in sgs_seats.R.
evidence.transfer: An event-window design needs forecast jumps from news plausibly unrelated to donor behaviour, and transaction-dated giving fine enough around each jump. The 2022 538 run timestamps could support a search, which stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062) and names its window and denominator. A Wald ratio needs a donor-side response series that the paper does not have.

evidence.title: Partisan Impacts on the Economy: Evidence from Prediction Markets and Close Elections
evidence.claim: Partisan shock is the indicator of a Republican president minus the pre-election prediction-market probability of a Republican president. Table 3, 1880-2004: coefficient 0.0255 (SE 0.0082) without the incumbent term and 0.0248 (SE 0.0084) with it; incumbent-party term -0.0046 (SE 0.0084). Congressional control could not be tested because markets did not track it before 1994 (fn 19).
evidence.system_side: SHIFT in sgs_panel.R builds exp_shift as expected Democratic control minus current Democratic control, the Democratic-sign version. The brain study contract defines Shift as P minus RMajNow with P the Republican majority probability. Preview: chamber-stacked -0.04, p 0.76 (2021-25).
evidence.transfer: Shift is an expected change in control before the election. The paper's shock is realized outcome minus prior expectation, so it transfers only to post-election giving. Independent shocks equal the number of elections, so any estimate is few-cluster and must say so. The sign convention must be stated as Democratic control, not Republican P.

evidence.title: Request for Review: Industry Economic Performance and Political Spending
evidence.claim: Pooled sector-FE models: (1) log Contrib on G(t-1), G(t), Neg(t-1), Midterm, Pres, Tossup, Trend; (2) RShare by chamber on growth, Shift, RMajNow, Midterm, Pres; (3) log Lobby on lagged log Lobby, growth, Neg, Unified. Growth z-scored within sector; CPI-deflated dollars; wild cluster bootstrap by sector; proposed sample 2008-2025 with 5 initial sectors (expansion to about 70 BEA industries allowed).
evidence.system_side: sgs_registry.R builds C1-C3 and L1-L3 as sector-FE tests with wild cluster restricted bootstrap by sector (Webb six-point weights); sgs_estimate.R header confirms this inference. Growth z-scoring and log DVs not checked in code here (the registry default DV is levels; see next bearing).
evidence.transfer: Holds only as a statement of the memo design. The build departs from it (next bearing), so build results must not be read as memo tests.

evidence.title: Request for Review: Industry Economic Performance and Political Spending
evidence.claim: Both growth timings belong in one regression (distributed lag) because separate models would each pick up part of the other effect. Totals get Tossup = 1 - abs(2P - 1), not a signed Republican-gains term. A Neg dummy, a Trend and lagged log lobbying are included. Lobbying uses Unified control.
evidence.system_side: Registry runs C1, C2 and C3 as separate single-growth models, not jointly. Contribution controls are pres_year, midterm_year, exp_dem_house, exp_dem_senate; the core has no Tossup, Neg or Trend term. Lobbying adds cur_dem_house and cur_dem_senate and has no lagged DV. Contribution DV defaults to real dollar levels (contributions_real_m), with logs only in robustness. Primary window 2020-2025 (R8). The g_pos/g_neg asymmetry split is an EXTENSION family from the 2026-09-26 rulings, not the core spec, so the rel statement that decline years use it as the core is softened. The expected-control terms are not P in levels: per year they come from an IEM annual mean, a binary forecaster final call (Democrats at or above 218 House or 51 Senate seats), or a market snapshot. The 2023 value is a final call flagged as measured Nov 2024, after the year.
evidence.transfer: Applies to every CORE C and L result. Rulings R4-R8 and the 2026-09-26 rulings may supersede parts of the memo, but results from separate-timing, signed-control models should not be reported as tests of memo H1 or H3.

evidence.title: Request for Review: Industry Economic Performance and Political Spending
evidence.claim: Probability of majority control is the preferred projected-control measure because access comes with majority status (Cox and Magar 1999, about 36,000 USD per member, cited and not verified here). Expected seat change is kept only as a robustness check. Q4 asks how quickly PAC giving tracks changing expectations within a cycle; Q7 asks about an event study around expected flips.
evidence.system_side: SEATS-W is a weekly test in report 221444: 17 weeks, 2022 House only (2020 and 2024 not usable yet). Dependent variable is the Democratic share of gross positive receipts. Regressor is the prior-week change in 538 Lite expected Democratic seats, with a week-of-cycle trend. House level, pooled-dollar (the first row of the primary table): -3.36 pp per seat, block-bootstrap p 0.11 and 0.10, not significant. The -3.47 pp figure with p 0.0086 and 0.0174 (Holm 0.034 and 0.070) is the equal-sector variant. Senate level is null in both weightings (equal-sector +6.23, p 0.65; pooled-dollar +3.99, p 0.81).
evidence.transfer: Exploratory, one-cycle reading only, 2022 House. The report itself calls it EFFECTIVELY A ONE-ELECTION TEST. Any headline must state the weighting; the pooled-dollar result is not significant.

evidence.title: Industry Growth and Political Spending: Research Plan
evidence.claim: Six core tests C1-C3 (contributions) and L1-L3 (lobbying), each with prior actual, same-year actual or predicted growth as the regressor; Y in millions of 2025 USD; X in percentage points; keep all six results including nulls; nine planned sectors give few independent groups so ordinary independent-row OLS errors are not sufficient for strong significance claims.
evidence.system_side: R build runs C1-C3 on contributions_real_m and L1-L3 on lobbying DVs with the growth regressors in SGS_GROWTH; controls are pres_year, midterm_year, exp_dem_house, exp_dem_senate, plus cur_dem_house and cur_dem_senate for lobbying; sector baselines; inference is wild cluster restricted bootstrap-t by sector with Webb six-point weights, enumerated when 6^G is at most 9999; Holm adjustment across pre-specified families. Main outcomes are levels in millions; log DVs appear only as robustness variants R-log and R-logFE on L-LV. No Tossup or trend regressor is in either control set.
evidence.transfer: Direct for the six-test design and the inference rules. The plan asks for dollar levels as the main outcome, and the build keeps levels as the main outcome too, so the log departure is a robustness addition, not the main model. Label any log-based figure as robustness.

evidence.title: Industry Growth and Political Spending: Research Plan
evidence.claim: Readiness check: verified contribution years overlap the IEM congressional forecasts only in 2021-2022; IEM covers 2008-2022 with 2023-2025 missing; a later election result must never substitute for a missing forecast.
evidence.system_side: Build fills 2023-2026 expected control from the 02 expected_control_2023_2026 sheet on Paul's ruling, labelled RETROSPECTIVE / NOWCAST (RETRO_LABEL), with exp_dem_*_after_year flags; STRICT variants drop values measured after their year; the 538 generic-ballot margin is robustness family H4-538 only, replacing exp_dem_house there and never the main measure.
evidence.transfer: Holds for the main series only as the labelled RETROSPECTIVE / NOWCAST measure that Paul ruled. Any quoted main-series result using 2023-2026 expectations must carry that label. The STRICT variant is the timing-clean check that the plan's rule supports, and it should be quoted beside any main-series result.

evidence.title: Industry Growth and Political Spending: Research Plan
evidence.claim: Do not add a full set of year indicators while keeping national annual controls because year effects absorb them; a separate check may swap the controls for year indicators to see whether the growth relationship survives common yearly shocks.
evidence.system_side: Build runs a year-FE variant of L1-LV..L3-LV as robustness (R-yearFE). Recorded reference values for L3-LV in sgs_review.R: base +0.352 (n 77); year-FE -0.477; log-FE -0.006; first-difference -0.537 (n 71); adjusted R2 0.884717 with growth and 0.884690 without, on the same rows. Other year-effect strata are marked insufficient because year effects leave no within-sector variation in a sector-only regression.
evidence.transfer: The recorded figures are hard-coded reference values from the Codex methodology review of run analysis-R-20260926T070630Z, which the pipeline must reproduce; they are not a fresh re-estimation in this check. The pooled slope is UNSTRATIFIED unless the per-sector SLOPES strata are quoted beside it. Single analysis path, so UNVERIFIED under DE-062.

evidence.title: Industry Growth and Political Spending: Research Plan
evidence.claim: Partisan direction is tested with a per-chamber Democratic share D over (D plus R), with zero denominators set missing; party, presidential and other committee flows are not assigned to a chamber without a defensible mapping.
evidence.system_side: SHIFT and DS families use per-chamber Democratic share. In the latest R report the core SHIFT-House and SHIFT-Senate are NOT ESTIMABLE; only the preview SHIFT-Chamber-PV is estimable (-0.0425, p 0.7576, 80 rows, 4 residual df, below the 6-year minimum and labelled post-result exploratory). SEATS-W House level on 538 lite, exploratory, 17 weeks, gives -3.4686 in one row of the report; 538 classic gives -3.58 in the same report.
evidence.transfer: The plan supplies only the outcome definition. SEATS-W and the SHIFT tests are extensions beyond the plan's annual design. The SHIFT preview is exploratory and below the 6-year minimum, so it must not be quoted as an annual test result. The 2022-only window for SEATS-W is not confirmed by the report.

evidence.title: Review: industry growth and political spending
evidence.claim: Main model should be log S_it = alpha_i + lambda_t + beta g_(i,t-1) with sector effects and full year effects, raw percent growth and log dollars; dynamic and other terms only as sensitivities.
evidence.system_side: Core tests use lagged raw growth (growth_previous_year_pct) on dollar-level outcomes with national controls pres_year, midterm_year, exp_dem_house, exp_dem_senate and no year effects. Year-FE, log and log-FE forms exist only as ROBUSTNESS variants R-yearFE, R-log, R-logFE. The L3-LV sign flip (+0.352 to -0.477 with sector+year FE; log-FE -0.006) is recorded in the brain note of 2026-09-26, not in code.
evidence.transfer: Same study and panel. The review predates the 2026-09-25 rulings; promoting the year-FE log model to primary is Paul's decision, as the review itself says.

evidence.title: Review: industry growth and political spending
evidence.claim: A contraction indicator estimates a level jump at zero, not an asymmetric slope; define contraction on raw growth below zero and use g+ = max(g,0) and g- = max(-g,0) with separate coefficients.
evidence.system_side: The ASYM family splits growth into _pos = max(g,0) and _neg = min(g,0) with a bootstrap equality test. CONTRACT-a and CONTRACT-b keep contracted_prior = 1(g<0) and the registry labels it a level shift. Contraction is defined on raw growth_previous_year_pct. Built _neg is non-positive, so the distress hypothesis predicts a negative slope, the opposite sign to the review's g- coefficient.
evidence.transfer: Direct. The sign must be flipped when comparing the built _neg slope with the review's g- coefficient. Both ASYM and CONTRACT are EXTENSION labels, not primary.

evidence.title: Review: industry growth and political spending
evidence.claim: f(P-M)+gM equals fP+(g-f)M, so Shift adds no information beyond P and current control M; a test of current versus expected power needs both terms in the model.
evidence.system_side: exp_shift = exp_dem minus cur_dem is built per chamber (sgs_panel.R:230-235). The contribution core controls carry exp_dem but not cur_dem, so H4shift-C enters exp_shift alone and cannot separate P from M in that model. For lobbying the code notes that cur_dem is retained and the shift terms reparametrise the core model. SHIFT preview over 2021-25, chamber-stacked: -0.04, p 0.76 (brain note, run analysis-R-20260926T070630Z).
evidence.transfer: Holds whenever a year-level probability enters with or without current control; within-chamber year effects would absorb both terms anyway. H4shift is labelled EXPLORATORY in code.

evidence.title: Review: industry growth and political spending
evidence.claim: The main campaign outcome should be corporate and trade-association PAC disbursements to congressional candidates, with individual, party, super PAC and independent-expenditure channels separate; never combine donor-to-PAC receipts with PAC-to-candidate payments.
evidence.system_side: Ruling R4 sets contributions = Mentat general giving across all recipient categories (DV label general giving (04), all recipient categories). The 2026-09-26 ruling keeps non_giving other-receipt rows, for example Stripe 464K to NRSC in 2021-22, in every test. Workbook 08 (README window 2019-2026, 2019-2020 missing): 5.6 percent of general-giving dollars reach House or Senate candidate committees. Company-PAC gifts are 8.84 percent of 2021-25 nominal giving, per the overlap check.
evidence.transfer: Paul's rulings govern scope. The review's point bears on how C1-C3 are read as a capacity mechanism and on the mixed receipt types, not on whether the series is collected.

evidence.title: Review: industry growth and political spending
evidence.claim: With five to ten sectors, report small-sample cluster corrections, restricted wild-cluster inference, cluster leverage and leave-one-sector-out checks; bootstrap p-values are not a guarantee; Driscoll-Kraay only as sensitivity with about 18 years.
evidence.system_side: Every focal term uses a wild cluster restricted bootstrap-t with Webb six-point weights, clusters = sectors. sgs_descriptive_note marks a term descriptive when p below 2/6^G cannot be reached with G sectors. LOSO and LOYO variants are built. No Driscoll-Kraay estimator appears in sgs_estimate.R (grep returned no match). Cluster leverage was not located in the lines read.
evidence.transfer: Direct. The review's point that no method repairs few independent units applies to every pooled growth coefficient.

evidence.title: Review: industry growth and political spending
evidence.claim: Some 538 models use fundraising, so explaining contributions with them creates a feedback problem; prefer polls-only. More monthly rows improve timing resolution, not the number of independent elections (about 9 elections, 6 flips): exploratory.
evidence.system_side: SEATS-W uses 538 Lite as primary. The code says Lite is not polls-only (it imputes unpolled races) but omits the Classic and Deluxe fundraising fundamentals. Rows are gated on available_at. Reported estimate, House 2022, 17 weeks, Lite: -3.47 pp D share per expected D seat, block-bootstrap p 0.0086 (3-week) and 0.0174 (5-week); the Holm-adjusted values 0.034 and 0.070 are in the brain note. Labelled one election and EXPLORATORY in code notes.
evidence.transfer: Holds until 2018 and 2020 weekly money joins; even then each further cycle adds one independent election, per the code notes.

evidence.title: Sector growth and political spending: source check (START HERE)
evidence.claim: Six core tests: Spending(sector, year) = sector baseline + b x Growth(sector, year-k) + c PresidentialYear + d MidtermYear + e ExpectedDemHouse + f ExpectedDemSenate, with k = 0 or k = 1, plus two predicted-growth tests; each run for contributions and lobbying; 72 sector-years (4 sectors x 2008-2025); no regressions run yet.
evidence.system_side: sgs_registry.R encodes the same growth variables (growth_previous_year_pct, growth_same_year_pct, predicted_growth_pct), the same four core controls (pres_year, midterm_year, exp_dem_house, exp_dem_senate) and sector fixed effects. The lobbying specification adds cur_dem_house and cur_dem_senate (SGS_L_CONTROLS, line 34), which the note treats as optional rather than core.

The primary sector-year window is 2020-2025 with at least 6 distinct years (SGS_WINDOW_RULE, sgs_registry.R lines 17-18; ruling R8 per sgs_config.R line 34), with a fallback of 10 consecutive years inside 2008-2025 only if the primary fails. The LobbyView tests use the 2008-2025 fallback. The claim that same-year growth is outside a real forecast's information set is not in the note and could not be verified, so it is removed.

evidence.title: Sector growth and political spending: source check (START HERE)
evidence.claim: Real growth = 100 x (rev_t / rev_t-1 - 1) on IBISWorld constant-price revenue with no further CPI adjustment. Spending in 2025 dollars = nominal x 321.9 / CPI_year. Democratic share = D / (D + R) by chamber, missing when the denominator is zero. Blanks stay missing, never zero.

Those lines do not show the zero-denominator missing rule, the growth formula or the CPI multiplier; those were not confirmed in this pass.
evidence.transfer: IBISWorld covers whole industries while Mentat contributions cover a roster of companies, a population mismatch the note does not state. The attribution of this mismatch to ruling 6 is not in the note and was not verified. IBISWorld historical values may include estimates and later revisions (text line 38).
